findings.text: Anger comes where a lifted state is checked: the heart lifted by strength (Uzziah), the merry heart (Ahasuerus), the glad heart (Haman), the heart already set (Dan 11:28).
Anger lodges and is cherished, and the lodging is the fool's.
Fear and anger follow one another: anger at God, then fear of God (2Sa 6:8–9); fear first, then anger at a weaker target (Dan 11:30).
The enemy's anger as the one attacked bears it: swallowing, grudge, venom in speech; felt as "my heart is in anguish within me" (Psa 55:4); answered by calling on God.
Put off what the wrath comes on, including one's own anger (Col 3:6 then 3:8).
The one refusal in God's own seat: "my heart would not turn toward this people" (Jer 15:1). It is not hardening.

Seat (v2): none in-verse or ±2. The next verse after Song 1:6 has "you whom my soul loves" (Song 1:7). Genuine. The bearer's own. The one who bears her brothers' anger turns at once to the one her soul loves.

In the verse: Job 36:13 "heart" (lev). The bearer's own. Genuine. A v3 §2.1 read it as human anger in the inner seat. G v3 §16.5 read it with 36:14 as death as accountability. Both stand. The phenomenon adds only that the heart here is where anger is kept, not where it flares.

Outside the verse: Ecc 7:8 "patient in spirit … proud in spirit". Genuine. Pro 6:32 "he who does it destroys himself" (nephesh). Genuine. The adulterer's own self, two verses before the husband's fury. The fury of Pro 6:34 is the other party's answer to one who has already destroyed his own soul.
2Ch 16:9 "those whose heart is blameless toward him". Genuine. It is the seer's diagnosis just before Asa's rage. The rage is at being told where his heart failed.
Beside: Num 24:13, Balaam: "to do either good or bad of my own will [heart]". Genuine, but the other party's. Balak's anger meets a heart subordinated to the word.

Est 7:5 "dared" (literally "whose heart has filled him to do this"). The offender's heart, as the king asks about it. Genuine. New here (no batch cites it). The king's wrath two verses later is aimed at the heart that dared.

1Sa 20:4 "Whatever you say [your soul says], I will do for you". Genuine. The other party's (David's), pledged to by Jonathan. New here. It stands three verses before 1Sa 20:7: Jonathan binds himself to David's soul just before they plan how to read Saul's anger. This adds to F v4 §1.1 (Jonathan and David) without changing it.

Gen 41:8 "his spirit was troubled". Genuine. The bearer's own (Pharaoh's), though in a different scene from his anger. The same king appears once with an angry act and once with a troubled spirit. The seat word comes with the trouble, not with the anger.
After, Job 32:8: "it is the spirit in man, the breath of the Almighty, that makes him understand". Genuine. Elihu justifies speaking despite his youth.

Further on, Job 32:18: "the spirit within me constrains me". Genuine, the bearer's own. New here (outside the ±3 window; read in this session). The seat of Elihu's released anger arrives as a spirit under pressure, with the belly as its bodily image.

Gen 34:8 "The soul of my son Shechem longs for your daughter". Genuine, but the offender's. The indignation of the brothers and the desire of the offender's soul stand side by side in consecutive verses.

Exo 11:10 "the Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart". Genuine. The offender's heart, hardened. New here (no batch cites it). Moses's hot anger (11:8) is set between God's announcement and the heart that will not yield.

2Sa 13:20 "do not take this to heart" (Absalom to Tamar). Genuine. The victim's, told to suppress. 2Sa 13:39 "spirit of the king". Genuine. The bearer's own, the angry king's spirit after the killing, turned to longing (G v3 §16.6; H v1 §1.3, "the Absalom arc"). New here is only the link back to the anger at 13:21.

2Sa 12:3, 8 "arms" (chêq, bosom): the lamb "lie in his arms", and "your master's wives into your arms". Relational and bodily, not inner. The parable's bosom and David's bosom are the same word: that is how the parable catches him. This is noted as a link, not as a seat.
Neh 5:5 "our flesh is as the flesh of our brothers" is kinship-sense. Spurious as a seat (H v1 §1.10 fringe).
Act 16:18 "spirit" is the spirit of divination addressed, not Paul's. Spurious for the bearer. The other party's (demonic) (compare M20 v3's Rev 2:17 row). New here, and not in any batch.

Job 6:11 "that I should be patient" (literally lengthen my nephesh). Genuine. The bearer's own. New here is only the pairing with vexation: vexation shortens the soul. Compare "slow to anger" = "long of nostrils" (pilot §2.2).
Job 17:4 "you have closed their hearts to understanding". Genuine, but the friends'.

Ecc 1:16–17 "I said in my heart … I applied my heart to know". Genuine. The bearer's own (E v2 §1.3; B v3 §1.2, §1.11; C v3 §10). New here is only the link: the heart that seeks knowledge comes before the vexation that knowledge brings.
Ecc 7:2, 7:4 "lay it to heart … the heart of the wise is in the house of mourning". Genuine.
Ecc 11:9 "let your heart cheer you". Genuine.
Psa 31:7 "you have known the distress of my soul". Genuine.
Outside the verse: no seat in Gen 45:2–9 or Job 18:1–7.
Num 27:11 "kinsman" (she'er, flesh). Kinship-sense. Spurious.
First: "Ps 95:8 refers to God, and David's plea to not harden Gods heart …", which kept it divine.

Outside the verse: Num 11:12 "Carry them in your bosom, as a nurse carries a nursing child". The bearer's own, relational and bodily. Moses's displeasure (11:10) comes out as a protest about the bosom he is asked to carry the people in (E v2 data note). Num 11:13 "meat" is spurious.

Outside the verse: Jon 4:3 "my life" and Jon 4:8 "that he might die" (nephesh). The bearer's own. Life-sense, as the thing asked to be ended. Jonah's anger takes his own nephesh as its object. This links to §9: anger turned on oneself.
Num 23:10 "Let me [my nephesh] die the death of the upright". Genuine. The would-be pronouncer's own.
Job 19:27 "My heart [kidneys] faints within me". Genuine. The bearer's own, Job's, just before his warning. New here. Job 19:26 "in my flesh" is bodily, the flesh in which he will see God.

The seat-sense question these verses raise: where the Spirit is the seat word, the seat is God's, and the anger is the human's. This matches M20 v3 §20's Eze 39:29 row: "God's, received by Israel: the human side is the receiving".
Outside the verse: Eze 32:10 "his own life". Life-sense.
1Cor 3:1 "spiritual". Not an inner seat of the quarrellers. Not in any batch.

2Ti 2:22 "a pure heart". Genuine. The remedy's site. The seat appears as the remedy (the pure heart, the Spirit) or as the victim (the naive heart). The quarreller's own source is named as passions, flesh or conceit, not as a seat word. This parallels M20 v3 §20 point 2: the seat as the site of the remedy.
Outside the verse: Pro 26:23 "fervent lips with an evil heart". Genuine. The whisperer's (D v2 §2.2; M20 v3 §14).
Pro 14:30 "a tranquil heart gives life to the flesh". Genuine.
Pro 17:27 "a cool spirit". Genuine (B v3 §1.6, §4.3).

Outside the verse: Pro 25:13 "he refreshes the soul of his masters" (a faithful messenger), two verses before 25:15. Genuine. The master's soul, as what is refreshed. The one who turns a ruler's anger by patience is the one who refreshes the ruler's soul. This is a neighbourhood observation, marked [Claude reading].
Psa 58:2 and 140:2 "hearts … heart". Genuine. The enemy's own, where the wrong is devised.

1. Part A: seven of the nine are genuine. Num 11:33 is spurious and Job 4:9 is divine. Six of the seven are a particular person's seat: three are Hezekiah's own heart in his two episodes (2Ch 29:10; 32:25–26), one is the provoker's heart (Solomon), one is the receiving spirit (Job), and one is another person's glad heart (Aaron). The seventh, Num 16:22, is God's relation to every human spirit.
Scarcity: "the land could not support both of them" (Gen 13:6), and "strife between the herdsmen" (13:7).
Rival claims on a person: "Why have our brothers the men of Judah stolen you away?" (2Sa 19:41).
What it leads to. Separation in peace (Gen 13:11), a boundary kept (Deu 2), or words growing fiercer (2Sa 19:43).
Amo 1:9 names the same failure for Tyre: "did not remember the covenant of brotherhood".
For the godless: "They die in youth" (Job 36:14).
Eliphaz sets this beside "man is born to trouble as the sparks fly upward" (Job 5:7). Trouble is universal, but dying of vexation is the fool's.
Or being turned round by the lowly. The donkey speaks (Num 22:28). Naaman's servants say "My father … will you not do it?" (2Ki 5:13), and he is restored.
The anger is answered by "prudence and discretion" (Dan 2:14): Daniel's.
Nebuchadnezzar "in furious rage" at the three who "do not serve your gods" (Dan 3:12–13).

Anger acting covertly: Zebul, "when [he] heard the words of Gaal … his anger was kindled. And he sent messengers to Abimelech secretly" (Judg 9:30–31). Anger turned into an ambush plan, "set an ambush in the field" (9:32).
In Joseph's story the anger that imprisons also positions. "The Lord was with Joseph" in the prison (Gen 39:21), and the officers imprisoned by Pharaoh's anger bring about Joseph's release (41:9–13).
Elihu burns with anger three times (Job 32:2, 3, 5). Then comes a long speech (32:6 onward).

Abner: a sworn switch of allegiance, "God do so to Abner … if I do not accomplish for David what the Lord has sworn" (2Sa 3:9). The one who charged him is silenced: "Ish-bosheth could not answer Abner another word, because he feared him" (3:11).
Jonathan seeing the spear thrown at himself (1Sa 20:33).
David hearing a parable (2Sa 12:1–4).
Public action: Nehemiah's "great assembly" and charge (Neh 5:7–9).

Vengeance with deceit: the brothers "answered Shechem … deceitfully" (Gen 34:13), and "Simeon and Levi … took their swords and came against the city while it felt secure and killed all the males" (34:25). This is the deed Jacob's curse names in §10.
being made "a byword of the peoples" (Job 17:6).
Or a plea to be allowed to die: "that it would please God to crush me, that he would let loose his hand and cut me off!" (Job 6:9).
New here: in Qoheleth the heart is where vexation stays at night (2:23) and where it must be removed from (11:10). In 7:3, though, the heart is what gains from sorrow.
Psa 10:13 "say in his heart". The offender's.
rebels refusing to come: "We will not come up" (Num 16:12–14).
What it leads to. Destruction of the object (Exo 32:20), purge and execution (Num 31:17), a lesser victory (2Ki 13:19), or approval once the explanation is heard (Lev 10:20).

Where it comes from. Thirst, and doubt of God's presence (17:1–7). For Moses and Aaron, "Because you did not believe in me" (Num 20:12). The people's quarrel is answered in the leaders by unbelief, and the leaders' act at the rock (20:10–11: "Hear now, you rebels", striking twice) takes the quarrel into themselves.
A burden shared: Moses (H v1 §3.3, "Moses' burden, then the Spirit shared", Num 11:10–17).
With a turned wish: the hired curser ends by wishing for the end of those he was hired to curse, "Let me die the death of the upright" (Num 23:10; G v3 §16.2; H v1 §6.5).
With Job's own hope, just before: "yet in my flesh I shall see God … My heart faints within me!" (Job 19:26–27).
What it leads to. Blessing instead of curse (Num 23:11). The judgment turned back on the pursuers (Job 19:29).
Hearing (1Sa 11:5–6: "they told him the news of the men of Jabesh").
Betrayal (Judg 14:16–18: the riddle given away through his wife).

Seeing: an Israelite brought a Midianite woman "in the sight of Moses and … the whole congregation … while they were weeping" (Num 25:6). "When Phinehas … saw it, he rose … and took a spear" (25:7), and killed them both (25:8).
Victory in battle (2Ch 28:6–8).

Directions of flow: Batch A §2.4 read 1Sa 11:5–7 as "hearing → Spirit → anger → act → dread spreading to the people", in contrast with 1Sa 18:8–10: "jealous anger → a harmful spirit → a spear". Both stand. New here: Judg 14:19 runs Spirit → killing → hot anger afterwards. The anger is the aftermath of a Spirit-driven act, not its cause, and it comes out as going home, not as more violence.
A covenant of peace for Phinehas (Num 25:12–13).
Compare Deu 32:29, "If they were wise, they would understand this".
The spear, twice (1Sa 18:11; 20:33).
A plan of genocide (Est 3:6–8).
On the other side, prayer and a guard (Neh 4:9), and building on regardless: "the people had a mind to work" (4:6).
It divides by allegiance: "there is quarreling among you … each one of you says, 'I follow Paul,' or 'I follow Apollos'" (1Cor 1:11–12).

With its named opposites: "that there be no divisions among you, but that you be united in the same mind and the same judgment" (1Cor 1:10); "godliness with contentment is great gain" (1Ti 6:6); "the Lord's servant must not be quarrelsome but kind to everyone … correcting his opponents with gentleness" (2Ti 2:24–25); "keep in step with the Spirit" (Gal 5:25).
Gal 5:24–25 "flesh … Spirit".
In the next verses, with a tranquil heart: "A tranquil heart gives life to the flesh, but envy makes the bones rot" (Pro 14:30).
A "cool spirit" belongs to the "man of understanding" (Pro 17:27).
"a debased mind" given up to by God (Rom 1:28).
"make no provision for the flesh" (Rom 13:14).
"put on the Lord Jesus Christ" (Rom 13:14).
What it leads to. "those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God" (Gal 5:21). Paul fears having to "mourn over many" (2Cor 12:21).

What it leads to. Arrest (Act 4:3), the reframing (above), and in Joh 7:25, the people's question, "Is not this the man whom they seek to kill?". The indignation borders on the plan to kill. Compare Mar 3:6 (§32).
"you who received the law … and did not keep it" (Act 7:53).
"in your hearts you devise wrongs" (Psa 58:2).
What it leads to. Release: "He who is bowed down shall speedily be released" (Isa 51:14). Endurance (Heb 11:27), and a test passed (Dan 1:12).

How it co-exists. With the tongue, which carries it (Hos 7:16; Isa 16:6 "boasting"). With the prophet's own wailing: "Therefore I wail for Moab … More than for Jazer I weep for you" (Jer 48:31–32); "let Moab wail for Moab" (Isa 16:7). God knows the insolence ("I know his insolence", Jer 48:30), and the prophet weeps over its end.
Where it comes from. A will to see another's nakedness (Hab 2:15). For Babylon, luxury and trade ("the merchants of the earth have grown rich", 18:3).
What it leads to. Shame (Hab 2:16), and Babylon's fall ("Fallen, fallen", Rev 14:8; 18:2). The call: "Come out of her, my people" (18:4).
Drawing near "with a true heart" (Heb 10:22).

What it leads to. "At every point you have proved yourselves innocent in the matter" (2Cor 7:11). The comfort of the other: "his spirit has been refreshed by you all" (7:13). Meeting together and encouraging (Heb 10:25).
The good provoking is set after a heart made clean (Heb 10:22), just as the bad strife of §19 is set after passions within (Jam 4:1).
"the haughtiness of his heart" (Jer 48:29) before Moab's insolence.

Where it comes from. From knowing the distance and asking anyway. Abraham says twice, "I have undertaken to speak to the Lord, I who am but dust and ashes" (Gen 18:27; 18:31). Gideon has already had his sign (Judg 6:38). The asker knows that the request presses on God's patience.
Every request is granted, and no anger comes. "I will not do it, if I find thirty there" (Gen 18:30); "God did so that night" (Judg 6:40). The anger feared never appears in either passage.
What it leads to. The asker stops. Abraham stops at ten and "returned to his place" (Gen 18:33). The asker, not God, sets the limit ("but this once").

The anger is followed each time by a charge to hand on: "Encourage him" (Deu 1:38); "charge Joshua, and encourage and strengthen him" (3:28). In Exo 4 a partner is given, and in Deuteronomy a successor. The anger does not end the man's service. It reshapes it.

What it leads to. Moses speaks of his exclusion to the people as a warning to them. Deu 4:21–22 is followed at once by "Take care, lest you forget the covenant" (4:23) and "the Lord your God is a consuming fire" (4:24). His own bearing of the anger becomes his teaching.

Whose spirit is not determinable. The M47 spirit classification v2 marks Psa 106:33 as [U] (#1880 item C-R4; C v3 R4). It could be Moses' spirit embittered, or God's Spirit rebelled against (compare Isa 63:10). Either way, the verse ties Meribah to Moses' loss "on their account".

The enemy's own appetite. In the song, the enemy boasts, "my desire [nephesh] shall have its fill of them" (Exo 15:9), and is answered by the wind of God (15:10). The enemy's appetite and God's fury meet over the same people. Already read in F v4 §8.4 ("the enemy's soul and the pursued soul").
What it leads to. Praise (Exo 15), or deliverance (2Sa 22:17 onward, not read here).
The king who trusts: "the king trusts in the Lord … Your hand will find out all your enemies" (Psa 21:7–9). The king at God's right hand: "Your people will offer themselves freely" (110:3, 5).
The protected are the people the anger struck earlier: "the Lord binds up the brokenness of his people, and heals the wounds inflicted by his blow" (Isa 30:26).

Intercession sits alongside the intercessor's own anger. The same chapter has Moses' own anger breaking the tablets (Exo 32:19; U1 §11 LD; Deu 9:17). Moses is angry at the people and pleads for them against God's anger, within one episode.

What it leads to. The people are spared. In Deuteronomy, the memory of the intercession is itself turned into instruction (Deu 9:25–29, "So I lay prostrate …"), set against the people's claim to righteousness (§8).
absent: "there was no one to intercede" (Isa 59:16; §41).

The name is used at once, in the next breath, to ask: "pardon our iniquity and our sin" (Exo 34:9), with "for it is a stiff-necked people". The name and the people's stiff neck are put side by side by Moses himself. The same pairing returns in Neh 9:16–17.
What it leads to. Worship (Exo 34:8), pardon (Num 14:20), and confession (Neh 9).
The breaking out stops a celebration. "David and all the house of Israel were celebrating before the Lord" (2Sa 6:5; 1Ch 13:8).
Forgetting. "take care lest you forget the Lord" (Deu 6:12); "You were unmindful of the Rock that bore you, and you forgot the God who gave you birth" (Deu 32:18).
Intermarriage. "they would turn away your sons from following me" (Deu 7:4).

Distress. "In the time of his distress he became yet more faithless to the Lord — this same King Ahaz. For he sacrificed to the gods of Damascus that had defeated him" (2Ch 28:22–23). Distress drives Ahaz further from God, not back. Contrast §16, where distress leads to crying out.

Stubbornness, and not believing. "they would not listen, but were stubborn, as their fathers had been, who did not believe in the Lord their God" (2Ki 17:14); "I know how rebellious and stubborn you are" (Deu 31:27).
You become what you follow. "They went after false idols and became false" (2Ki 17:15). In exile "you will serve gods of wood and stone … that neither see, nor hear, nor eat, nor smell" (Deu 4:28).

What is known in the heart. Joshua ties the threat to what the people already know: "you know in your hearts and souls, all of you, that not one word has failed of all the good things … so the Lord will bring upon you all the evil things" (Jos 23:14–15). The heart's own knowledge of God's faithfulness is made the ground for believing the warning.

Deu 11:16 "lest your heart be deceived" (before) and 11:18 "lay up these words of mine in your heart and in your soul" (after). The deceived heart is the cause; the heart filled with the words is the guard. B v3 §4.1; C v3 §8.2; E v2 §4.1; G v3 §10; H v1 §5.1.
Deu 29:18–19 "whose heart is turning away" / "blesses himself in his heart … stubbornness of my heart". E v2 §4.1, §12; C v3 §9.1; F v4 §9.6. Pilot §1.6 reads 29:20 with it.
Jos 23:14 "you know in your hearts and souls". B v3 §1.1 ("the heart as the knower").
Lev 26:29–30 "flesh" (bodily) and "my soul will abhor you" (God's; F v4 §4).
Treachery like the fathers': "turned away and acted treacherously like their fathers; they twisted like a deceitful bow" (Psa 78:57).
Trust in man: "Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his strength, whose heart turns away from the Lord" (Jer 17:5).

From youth, turning the back: "done nothing but evil in my sight from their youth" (Jer 32:30); "They have turned to me their back and not their face … they have not listened to receive instruction" (32:33).
Discouraging the heart: the spies "discouraged the heart of the people of Israel from going into the land" (Num 32:9), and "the Lord's anger was kindled on that day" (32:10).
From ingratitude after being carried: "the Lord your God carried you, as a man carries his son … Yet … you did not believe" (Deu 1:31–32).
From not following wholly: "because they have not wholly followed me, none except Caleb … and Joshua … for they have wholly followed the Lord" (Num 32:11–12).
Spoken against: "Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant Moses?" And the anger of the Lord was kindled against them (Num 12:8–9). The charge is a lack of fear.

Silenced: Amaziah to the prophet: "Have we made you a royal counselor? Stop! Why should you be struck down?" (2Ch 25:16). The prophet stops, but says: "I know that God has determined to destroy you, because you have done this and have not listened to my counsel.".

Killed: after Jehoiada died, "the king listened to them [the princes]"; prophets "testified against them, but they would not pay attention"; Zechariah, whom "the Spirit of God clothed", was stoned "in the court of the house of the Lord" (2Ch 24:17–21).
From loss of the restraining figure: "after the death of Jehoiada the princes … paid homage to the king. Then the king listened to them" (2Ch 24:17).
How it co-exists. Aaron confesses at once: "Oh, my lord, do not punish us because we have done foolishly and have sinned" (Num 12:11). Amaziah does not.
What it leads to. Leprosy and intercession (Num 12:10–13), stoning (2Ch 24:21), and a determined end (2Ch 25:16).
How it co-exists. Weeping and zeal in one scene. The people are "weeping in the entrance of the tent of meeting" (Num 25:6) while the offender walks past with a Midianite woman, and Phinehas acts.
Where it comes from. From seeing. "as you see with your own eyes" (2Ch 29:8); "when they see the afflictions of that land" (Deu 29:22).

A song as witness. "write this song and teach it … that this song may be a witness for me against the people of Israel" (Deu 31:19). The explanation is given before the ruin, so that the ruin can be read when it comes.
What it leads to. Reform (Hezekiah, §22) or rebuilding (Ezr 5:13). In 2Ch 29 and Ezr 5, reading the ruin rightly is the first step back.
Where it comes from. From memory of shared punishment: "Have we not had enough of the sin at Peor from which even yet we have not cleansed ourselves" (Jos 22:17).
The accused answer by appealing to God's knowledge: "The Mighty One, God, the Lord! He knows; and let Israel itself know! If it was in rebellion … do not spare us today" (Jos 22:22).
What it leads to. The Gibeonites live as servants (Jos 9:21–23); justice is ordered (2Ch 19); the temple is provided for (Ezr 7).

Crying out: "when the people of Israel cried out to the Lord, the Lord raised up a deliverer" (Judg 3:9); "We have sinned against you, because we have forsaken our God" (10:10); "do to us whatever seems good to you. Only please deliver us this day" (10:15).
Seeking favour: "Jehoahaz sought the favor of the Lord, and the Lord listened to him, for he saw the oppression of Israel" (2Ki 13:4).

Relapsing: "whenever the judge died, they turned back and were more corrupt than their fathers … They did not drop any of their practices or their stubborn ways" (Judg 2:19); "Nevertheless, they did not depart from the sins of the house of Jeroboam" (2Ki 13:6).
The cry is answered while the relapse is foreseen. Nations are left "to test Israel by them" (Judg 2:22).
What it leads to. Rest "forty years" (Judg 3:11), then again.
"God has turned away from me and answers me no more" (1Sa 28:15).
Conscience afterwards: "David's heart struck him after he had numbered the people … 'I have sinned greatly … I have done very foolishly'" (2Sa 24:10).
Manasseh (context of §20): "when he was in distress, he entreated the favor of the Lord his God and humbled himself greatly … Then Manasseh knew that the Lord was God" (2Ch 33:12–13).
From the prophet's announcement (Rehoboam, 2Ch 12:5).
Humbling with a confession of God's justice: "The Lord is righteous" (2Ch 12:6); "you are just" (Ezr 9:15).

Humbling that is partial. Rehoboam is spared destruction but made to serve Shishak, "that they may know my service and the service of the kingdoms" (2Ch 12:8). Bronze shields replace gold (12:10). And "he did evil, for he did not set his heart to seek the Lord" (12:14). The humbling turned the wrath, and the heart was still not set.
The anger is turned (Rehoboam), deferred past the humbled one's lifetime (Hezekiah; Josiah, "your eyes shall not see all the disaster", 2Ki 22:20), or feared again (Ezra).
1Ki 8:47–48 / 2Ch 6:37–38 "turn their heart … with all their heart and with all their soul" (B v3 §5; C v3 §2.3, §8.1; D v2 §5; E v2 §13).
2Ki 22:19 / 2Ch 34:27 "your heart was penitent / tender".
2Ch 12:14 "did not set his heart to seek the Lord".
The formula: "the sins of Jeroboam, which he sinned and which he made Israel to sin" (1Ki 14:16; 15:30; 16:13, 26).
Self-sale: "you have sold yourself to do what is evil" (1Ki 21:20). "There was none who sold himself … like Ahab, whom Jezebel his wife incited" (21:25).
Lightness: "as if it had been a light thing for him to walk in the sins of Jeroboam" (1Ki 16:31).
The measure given is David's heart: "you have not been like my servant David, who … followed me with all his heart" (1Ki 14:8).
One found pleasing in a condemned house. Jeroboam's child "shall come to the grave, because in him there is found something pleasing to the Lord" (1Ki 14:13).
Recognition without turning. "Have you found me, O my enemy?" (1Ki 21:20). Ahab recognises the prophet as his enemy.
"it came to the point in Jerusalem and Judah that he cast them out from his presence" (2Ki 24:20).
From the king's heart hardened against turning: Zedekiah "stiffened his neck and hardened his heart against turning to the Lord" (2Ch 36:13).

God's compassion is named in the same passage as "no remedy": "The Lord … sent persistently to them by his messengers, because he had compassion on his people" (2Ch 36:15). The persistence of the compassion is what the mocking used up.
What it leads to. Josiah's death at Megiddo (2Ki 23:29), exile, and the burning of the temple (2Ch 36:17–19).
From reading the ruin (§12: 2Ch 29:8–9).
From awareness of accumulated guilt ("our guilt is already great", 2Ch 28:13; "we have greatly transgressed", Ezr 10:13).
